terms.grammar: relative pronoun, with a verb of its own
evidence: Hor. Ep. 1.2.14: quidquid dēlīrant rēgēs, plectuntur Achīvī
Cic. Att. 12.1.2: garrīmus quicquid in buccam
terms.comment: Both spellings of the neuter are ancient (Quint. 1.7.6). In its own Latin the house writes the assimilated quicquid; quotations keep their edition’s spelling.

terms.gloss: whatever, whichever (with a noun or alone)
evidence: Caes. BG 1.31.14: fortūnam, quaecumque accidat, experiantur
terms.comment: Cicero, Caesar and Sallust give it a verb of its own; “any … whatever” without one is Livy’s and later (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: quārē habē tibi quidquid hoc libellī quālecumque
phrases.english: so take this little book for your own, whatever it is, such as it is
whatever madness the kings commit, the Greeks pay for it

phrases.latin: quidquid est, ubicumque est, quodcumque agit, renīdet
phrases.english: whatever it is, wherever he is, whatever he is doing, he grins

phrases.latin: quidquid praecipiēs, estō brevis, ut citō dicta percipiant animī docilēs teneantque fidēlēs
phrases.english: whatever you teach, be brief, so that minds may grasp what is said quickly, learn it and keep it faithfully

phrases.latin: quid, cum cōram sumus et garrīmus quicquid in buccam?
phrases.english: and what about when we are together and chatter whatever comes into our heads?
